No real bank data appears anywhere in this repository. Every method here transfers unchanged to the real Tangerine dataset: only the input CSV path changes, because scripts/build_world.py already consumes either file.

f1StructuralVsDiscretionary.question: Which dollars are locked by the calendar and which are choices?
f1StructuralVsDiscretionary.method: Per category, build a daily spend series over the 365 day ledger, subtract the day of week mean effect and the holiday window mean effect (2025-11-15 to 2025-12-31), then compute lag autocorrelation at lags 28 to 35 (the monthly billing window). The significance threshold is max(1.96 / sqrt(365), p95 of the same series at control lags 50 to 180). A category with at least 20 debit rows whose peak exceeds the threshold is structural; every other category is discretionary. Structural share of annual spend is the sum of structural category annual spend divided by total annual spend.

limitations: Classification is per category, not per transaction: a category counts in full as structural or discretionary, so a category that mixes fixed bills with choices cannot be split internally.

The lag window tests monthly recurrence only. Weekly locked behavior (for example weekday commuting in Transit) counts as discretionary here by construction; F2 measures that weekly pattern separately.
One year of daily data gives 365 samples, so statistical power near the threshold is limited and a single billing drift can move a peak.
Travel has fewer than the minimum debit rows for the lag test and is counted as discretionary because it cannot demonstrate recurrence.
The mock ledger was generated with 28 to 32 day billing cycles, so this detector is validated against known construction rather than a real statement; the method itself does not use the generator.

f2Seasonality.question: When in the week and the year does this person actually spend?
f2Seasonality.method: Per category, annual spend is decomposed into day of week shares (7), ledger month shares (12), and the holiday window share versus the rest of the year; every share is compared with the share of days it covers. Verdict rules: holiday lift at or above 1.25 means calendar driven concentration; weekly deviation (weekend share versus its 2/7 calendar baseline, relative) at or above 0.2 means a behavioral rhythm, and only categories with at least 30 debit rows are eligible for that flag because sparse weekday patterns are sampling noise; both means mixed; neither means weak seasonality.

numbers.overallVerdict: mixed (calendar driven and behavioral, split by category)
numbers.verdictSummary: behavioral: Groceries; mixed (calendar driven holiday plus behavioral weekly rhythm): Dining, Transit; structural (calendar driven): Retail, Travel; weak or no seasonality: Subscriptions, Utilities

categories.name: Dining
categories.verdict: mixed (calendar driven holiday plus behavioral weekly rhythm)
categories.plainLanguage: Dining concentrates spend in the holiday window at 1.47 times its calendar share while its weekend share sits 24% away from the 2/7 calendar baseline, so the seasonality has both a calendar driven and a behavioral part.

categories.name: Groceries
categories.plainLanguage: Groceries follows a weekday and weekend rhythm: weekend share 34.5% versus a 28.6% calendar baseline (21% deviation), while its holiday lift of 1.08 stays near 1.00, so the seasonality tracks behavior, not fixed calendar dates.

categories.name: Retail
categories.plainLanguage: Retail puts 23.2% of annual spend into the 47 day holiday window (1.80 times its calendar share) while its weekend pattern stays near the calendar baseline, so the pattern follows the calendar rather than weekday habits.

categories.name: Subscriptions
categories.plainLanguage: Subscriptions shows neither holiday concentration (lift 0.97) nor a weekend shift (deviation 8%); spend spreads evenly across the year beyond its monthly recurrence measured in F1.

categories.name: Transit
categories.verdict: mixed (calendar driven holiday plus behavioral weekly rhythm)
categories.plainLanguage: Transit concentrates spend in the holiday window at 1.52 times its calendar share while its weekend share sits 36% away from the 2/7 calendar baseline, so the seasonality has both a calendar driven and a behavioral part.

categories.name: Travel
categories.plainLanguage: Travel has 7 debit rows, below the 30 row floor for a weekday reading, so only the calendar test applies: holiday lift 2.94 gives 'structural (calendar driven)'.

categories.name: Utilities
categories.plainLanguage: Utilities shows neither holiday concentration (lift 0.63) nor a weekend shift (deviation 3%); spend spreads evenly across the year beyond its monthly recurrence measured in F1.

limitations: Shares are computed over a single year, so month shares mix season with one off events: the Travel month shares come from seven rows, below the reliability floor for any weekday reading.
The holiday window (2025-11-15 to 2025-12-31, 47 days) is the mock generator's surge period; on real data the same rule should be rewritten against declared holiday dates before it is trusted.

Verdict thresholds (1.25 holiday lift, 0.20 weekend deviation, 30 row floor) are declared design choices, not hypothesis tests; nearby values would relabel borderline categories such as Dining (weekend deviation 0.24) and Groceries (0.21).
Day of week shares attribute spend to the posting date, not to the moment of consumption (a late night Saturday charge counts Saturday).
Calendar driven versus behavioral is an interpretation of the pattern, not a causal test of why the person spent.

Subscriptions and Utilities bill on fixed dates, so their calendar recurrence shows up in F1 while F2 correctly reports their seasonal shape as weak; recurrence and seasonality are different questions.

f3DeficitRisk.question: Can the ledger predict a deficit day before it happens?
f3DeficitRisk.method: L2 logistic regression (scikit-learn) on daily rows with trailing 7 and 30 day net flow, day of week and month indicators, days since payroll, and trailing 30 day spend volatility; every feature row uses only information available the night before day t (trailing windows end at t minus 1, days since payroll is measured through t minus 1, and the indicators are calendar facts known in advance), so day t never contributes to its own feature row; target is a same day negative closing balance. Time ordered split at 2026-02-01; C chosen by 3 fold time ordered CV inside the training window; metrics on the held out test segment.

numbers.targetDefinition: same day deficit: closing balance below 0 CAD on that calendar day (86 events in the ledger)
numbers.decisionRule: predicted deficit when probability is at or above 0.5
numbers.robustnessAlternativeTarget: next day closing balance below 1,000 CAD (threshold variant)

limitations: One synthetic account and one year of daily rows (364 samples, 86 events): uncertainty around the test AUC is wide and no confidence interval is claimed.

Strong concept drift: the account balance rises monotonically after the deficit season, so test months are out of distribution for the training months (train AUC versus test AUC in metrics shows the gap).
The current closing balance is excluded by design, which keeps the model honest as a forward screen but caps discrimination; an autoregressive balance feature would score much higher and say less.

Raw accuracy at the 0.5 threshold sits below the majority class baseline because the class balance shifts sharply between train and test; AUC is the headline metric and the confusion matrix is reported in full.
Correlation, not causation: coefficients describe association inside this ledger. days_since_payday raising the odds does not mean waiting longer causes a deficit.
Month indicators memorize this ledger's calendar (the November to April deficit season) and carry no meaning for another year.

f4PlaneChangeCost.question: What does it cost to move a category's spending onto the income phase (the plane change cost)?
f4PlaneChangeCost.definition: For a given category, every debit with pay cycle phase p (days since the most recent payroll deposit, with a virtual deposit anchored at 2025-10-25) of 7 or more is moved forward to (next payroll date) + (p mod 7) days, landing it in the first week after the following deposit; debits with phase 0 to 6 are already in the income window and do not move. The daily balance path is rebuilt from the same opening balance with identical amounts, and peak, trough, drawdown, and month end closes are recomputed over the 365 day ledger. The reverse direction is computed two ways: the observed ledger (left misaligned, delta zero by construction, benefit forgone equals the aligned delta) and an anti aligned stress case that moves every debit of the category to the day before the next deposit.
f4PlaneChangeCost.method: Rebuild the daily balance path for the 365 day ledger under each scenario from the same opening balance and identical amounts, sorted by (simulated date, original row order), then recompute peak, trough, drawdown (peak minus trough of daily closes) and all 12 month end closes. Deltas are scenario minus baseline, except drawdownImprovementCents, which is baseline minus scenario so a positive value always means a tighter drawdown.

limitations: This is a counterfactual simulation, not a causal estimate: real merchants, rent, and autopay bills cannot in general be moved to an arbitrary day, so the deltas bound an opportunity rather than measure an achievable effect.
Only timing moves: every scenario conserves the category total exactly, so an aligned scenario never improves the ledger by spending less.

Month end floors are sample points. The forward shift can only move a debit forward to days 25 to 31 of the deposit month, and a spill past a 30 day month lands on day 1 to 3 of the next month, so no month end close can ever fall under the aligned rule; the binding floor here is December, a 31 day month that no forward target can escape, which is why the floor delta is exactly zero while the true intra month trough (troughDeltaCents) moves. Floors respond to amounts, which is F5's capping intervention, not to timing.

The counterfactual holds behavior fixed: moving dining dates in the simulation does not change how much the person chooses to eat out, and the model assumes the person can and would move each payment.
Paydays are one monthly deposit on the 25th in this ledger; biweekly or weekly pay cycles would need a different phase definition, though the recipe (phase to deposit window) transfers unchanged.

Travel carries only seven debit rows, so its aligned delta is dominated by single splurges moving across the trough; read it as an upper bound on timing effects for rare large purchases rather than a habit effect.
Daily closing balances are the sampling grid: intra day ordering between a moved debit and the deposit itself is not modeled beyond the row order rule.

f5Interventions.question: Which intervention lifts the balance floor and tightens the drawdown the most?
f5Interventions.method: Each intervention rebuilds the 365 day balance path from the observed ledger with one rule applied, then recomputes peak, trough, drawdown and month end closes. Deltas are scenario minus baseline except drawdownImprovementCents (baseline minus scenario). Auto save uses the combined view (checking plus reserve); equality with the baseline is asserted in code.
f5Interventions.rankingRule: Primary key: minMonthEndDeltaCents descending. Secondary key: drawdownImprovementCents descending. rankByDrawdown gives the alternative ordering directly.

numbers.bestInterventionName: Cap the top surge category at its baseline rate

interventions.name: Cap the top surge category at its baseline rate
interventions.label: simulated counterfactual (not observed in the data)
interventions.definition: Retail has the largest holiday excess spend ($2,366.72 above its non holiday daily rate across the 47 day window); every Retail debit inside the window is scaled by 0.488597 so holiday spend equals $2,261.18, capped not removed, rounded to integer cents.
interventions.caveat: This is an amount change (spend less in the window), not a timing change, so it bounds a behavior change.

interventions.name: Realign Dining to the income phase
interventions.label: simulated counterfactual (not observed in the data)
interventions.definition: The largest discretionary category by annual spend (Dining, $27,766.09 per year) runs through the exact F4 alignment shift: debits with pay cycle phase 7 or more move to (next payday) + (p mod 7).
interventions.caveat: Same modeling choice and the same caveats as F4; timing only, amounts conserved exactly.

interventions.name: Consolidate subscriptions to a single cycle
interventions.label: simulated counterfactual (not observed in the data)
interventions.definition: Every detected recurring charge (111 debit rows from the 111 subscription runs in world.json provenance) moves to day 27 of its month, one billing cycle anchored two days after the 25th payday. Amounts unchanged.
interventions.caveat: Blends consolidation with a post payday anchor; the anchor day is part of the definition.

interventions.name: Fixed auto save on payday with emergency release
interventions.label: simulated counterfactual (not observed in the data)
interventions.definition: $1,000.00 leaves the checking account on every payroll deposit into an intervention reserve; any day whose close would fall below the deficit threshold draws from the reserve up to the threshold. Floor and drawdown are evaluated on the combined view (checking plus reserve), where a pure transfer is a declared null.
interventions.caveat: Combined view deltas are zero by construction; the full accounting (released days, lifted and created counts, reserve balance) is listed in auxiliary.

limitations: All four rows are simulated counterfactuals. Nothing here was observed; each delta is what the stated rule would produce under fixed behavior elsewhere in the ledger.
Ranking is by minimum month end balance first and drawdown improvement second; a different priority reorders the list, which is why rankByDrawdown ships alongside rank.
The surge cap changes amounts, not only timing: it models spending less during the holiday window, so its delta bounds a behavior change rather than a scheduling change.
The consolidation row blends two effects (one cycle plus a post payday anchor) because a single cycle must sit somewhere; the anchor day is stated in the definition rather than hidden.

The auto save row is an internal transfer: on the combined view of checking plus reserve the floor and the drawdown cannot move, which is a declared null, not an oversight. The deficit counts stay flat for an arithmetic reason: covering a genuine deficit day would require the held reserve to exceed itself plus the shortfall, because the holding that funds the release is what deepens the checking balance, so releases only reverse the dips the saving itself creates. The durable change is the reserve balance, reported in auxiliary.
Intervention interactions are not modeled: applying every rule at once is not the sum of the rows, because each scenario starts from the observed ledger.
All numbers come from the synthetic seed 20261107 ledger; deltas will differ on the real Tangerine dataset, though the simulation recipe is unchanged.
